appraisal_events.evidence: "Quel brave homme que votre père!... Eux et lui, quelles bonnes gens!" / "le duc de Guermantes n'eût pas eu d'hésitation à les recommander pour une place de jardiniers"
appraisal_events.explanation: The duke's ostensibly warm praise of Swann's family is exposed by the narrator as patronizing condescension, comparable to how the aristocracy speaks of any bourgeois family, subtly diminishing Swann's memory beneath the surface fondness.

appraisal_events.evidence: "voilà comment le faubourg Saint-Germain parle à tout bourgeois des autres bourgeois... pour l'humilier. C'est ainsi qu'un antisémite dit à un Juif... du mal des Juifs"
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator directly generalizes from the duke's remark to accuse this manner of speech of serving, alongside flattery, to humiliate, comparing it to antisemitic condescension, casting the duke in a critical light.

status_effects.explanation: The fond-seeming remembrance of Swann by the Guermantes is locally undercut by the narrator's exposure of its condescending, class-conscious undertone.
The narrator's pointed comparison of the duke's speech pattern to antisemitic condescension casts him critically, even as his own words remain superficially affable.

ambiguities: The blame in S2 is framed by the narrator as a trait of 'le faubourg Saint-Germain' generally, using the duke's remark as its exemplar, so attributing it specifically and individually to duc de Guermantes rather than to the aristocratic class as a whole is somewhat interpretive.

The passage's closing lines ('Swann était lié avec tous les gens de cette même société') can be read as the narrator affirming Swann's genuinely elevated social standing against the duchess's diminishing framing, creating a mixed rather than purely negative movement around Swann; a single diminishment event was judged the more conservative reading.
